mcqs.question: What must be true about an array for opposite-end two pointers to correctly solve a pair-sum problem on it?
options: The array must contain no duplicate values
There must be a provable rule for which pointer to move that never discards the true answer
The array must have an even number of elements
The target sum must be positive
mcqs.explanation: The pattern's correctness rests entirely on being able to prove that moving a specific pointer, given the current comparison, can never skip over the true answer — that's the monotonicity argument sorted order provides. Duplicates, parity, and sign of the target are unrelated to whether the pattern is valid.

mcqs.question: Why does the two-pointer palindrome check beat building `s[::-1]` and comparing it to `s`?
options: It avoids allocating a second full-length copy and can stop at the first mismatch
It has a better asymptotic time complexity
It works on strings containing unicode characters, unlike the reversed-copy approach
It avoids the need to know the string's length in advance
mcqs.explanation: Both approaches are O(n) time; the win is space (no second string) and the ability to short-circuit as soon as a mismatch appears near either end. Unicode handling and needing the length are unaffected by which approach you pick.

mcqs.question: In sorted-array Two Sum, `arr[left] + arr[right]` is smaller than the target. Why is it safe to advance `left` rather than move `right`?
options: Because arr[left] is the smallest remaining value, and if it can't reach the target with any remaining right value, it can never be part of a valid pair
Because moving right would risk an index-out-of-range error
Because the target is guaranteed to appear closer to the middle of the array
Because left must always move before right in this pattern
mcqs.explanation: Since the array is sorted, arr[left] paired with the current largest remaining value (arr[right]) is the best chance it has — if that's still too small, no smaller right value helps either, so arr[left] is provably useless going forward. There's no fixed move order and no index-safety issue driving the choice.

mcqs.question: You run the sorted-array Two Sum two-pointer logic directly on an unsorted array. What actually goes wrong?
options: The loop never terminates because left and right never converge
It throws an index-out-of-bounds exception on most inputs
It works correctly but runs in O(n²) instead of O(n)
The monotonicity assumption breaks, so a pointer can be advanced past the index a valid answer actually needed
mcqs.explanation: Without sorted order, "sum too big, move right down" is no longer a valid inference — a needed value could be sitting anywhere, so the pointer move can silently skip the true answer and return a wrong result (or none at all), not raise an error or just run slower. The loop still terminates in the same number of steps; it just isn't correct.

mcqs.question: Why can't you reverse a Python `str` in place with the swap-based two-pointer code shown for arrays?
options: Python strings are immutable, so index assignment on a str is not allowed
Python strings don't support indexing with two pointers
The swap would corrupt the string's internal length field
It works fine; the array version and string version are identical in Python
mcqs.explanation: str is an immutable type in Python, so `s[left] = s[right]` raises a TypeError regardless of the algorithm — you must convert to a list of characters first, reverse that, and rejoin, which costs its own O(n) time and space. Indexing itself works fine on strings; immutability is the actual blocker.
